clinician.trajectory_summary: A seven-year-old male child with a history of proximal tubular dysfunction presented with acute onset right-sided weakness, severe headache, photophobia, phonophobia, facial asymmetry, slurred speech, high fever (38.7C), irritability, and disorientation following superficial keratectomy. Initial physical examination revealed mild distress, irritability, and disorientation, with normal pupils and an otherwise unremarkable systemic exam. Vital signs showed fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and elevated blood pressure. Initial workup included an unremarkable CT brain and an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination after lumbar puncture, effectively ruling out structural lesions and CNS infection. Laboratory results showed mild electrolyte abnormalities (Na 150, K 3.1, HCO3 17, urea 90) and a normal CRP (0.3) with a slightly elevated WBC (11.4). The patient subsequently stabilized, pain was managed with supportive medications, and he was discharged home. The final impression was hemiplegic migraine, potentially triggered by emotional stress during anesthesia or abortive vasoconstrictive drugs.
